tips.title: One equation, three questions
tips.body:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$

Every question on this is that equation rearranged. Asked for the **actual size**, divide the image by the magnification. Asked for the **image size**, multiply. Write the equation down first every time and the rearranging stops being a guess.

tips.title: Put both lengths in the same unit first
tips.body: Magnification has **no unit**, because it is a length divided by a length — but only if both are measured **in the same unit**. An image in **mm** over an actual size in **µm** gives an answer a thousand times out. Convert **before** you divide, not after.

tips.title: Each step is a thousand
tips.body: **mm → µm → nm** each go **×1000**, because milli is $10^{-3}$, micro is $10^{-6}$ and nano is $10^{-9}$ — three powers of ten apart each time. So 1 mm = 1000 µm = 1 000 000 nm. Pico is $10^{-12}$, one more step down.

tips.title: Magnification and resolution are different things
tips.body: **Magnification** is how much bigger the image is. **Resolution** is the smallest gap that still shows as **two** things rather than one. Magnifying a blurred image just gives a bigger blur — which is exactly why the electron microscope mattered: it improved the **resolution**.

tips.title: A drawing is marked on its lines
tips.body: A biological drawing earns marks for **clear unbroken pencil lines**, **no shading**, **straight label lines that do not cross**, and a stated **magnification**. Drawing what you think should be there rather than what you can see loses marks for accuracy.

why.matters:
Biology is limited by what can be seen. Cells were not discovered by better thinking but by better lenses, and every organelle in the last topic was invisible until the instrument existed to show it.

So this topic is two things at once: the history of what a new technology does to a science, and the arithmetic that turns a picture into a **measurement**. A photograph of a cell tells you nothing about its size until you know the magnification.

examples.title: What the electron microscope let people see
examples.body:
A light microscope cannot resolve anything smaller than about **200 nm**, however much it magnifies — past that you are enlarging a blur. That single limit is why ribosomes, plasmids and the inside of a mitochondrion were unknown.

An electron microscope resolves to about **0.2 nm**, **1000 times** finer, and those structures appeared. Nothing about cells changed; what changed was the instrument. That is the specification's point about technology and understanding, and it is worth a mark on its own.

props.caption: The smallest detail each can separate. Smaller is better.

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion comparing resolution: a light microscope separating detail down to two hundred nanometres against an electron microscope at nought point two, a thousand times finer

examples.title: How big a cell actually is
examples.body:
The units are unfamiliar because the sizes are, and getting a feel for them stops a great many wrong answers. A cheek cell is about **60 µm** across — roughly the width of a hair. A bacterium is about **2 µm**, thirty times smaller. A ribosome is about **20 nm**.

Put those on the same scale and the ribosome disappears, which is exactly what it did under a light microscope: at 200 nm of resolution it is ten times too small to separate from anything near it.

props.caption: To scale, in nanometres. The ribosome is there.

visual.alt: Three bars drawn to true scale: a cheek cell at sixty micrometres, a bacterium at two micrometres and a ribosome at twenty nanometres, which is too small to see on the same scale

examples.title: Why a published photograph carries a scale bar
examples.body:
A micrograph in a journal is labelled with a **scale bar** rather than a magnification, and the reason is practical: the moment anyone reprints the image at a different size, the magnification printed beside it becomes a lie.

A scale bar is drawn **on** the image, so it is enlarged with it and stays correct. Measure the bar, read what it says it represents, and you can measure anything else in the picture. It is the same reason a map carries one, and it is why the exam gives you a scale bar and expects you to do the rest.

visual.alt: A table showing what happens when a micrograph is resized: a printed magnification becomes wrong as soon as the image is enlarged, while a scale bar drawn on the image grows with it and stays correct

steps.title: Why microscope technology mattered
steps.body:
**New technology changes what we can know.** The specification puts it directly: changes in microscope technology, including **electron microscopy**, have let us see cell structures and organelles **with more clarity and detail than in the past**, and so have **increased our understanding** of what sub-cellular structures do.

**Two different measures are improving here, and they are not the same thing.**

- **Magnification** — how many times **bigger** the image is than the object.
- **Resolution** — the **smallest distance between two points** that still appear as **two separate points**.

**Resolution is the one that limits you.** Magnify a blurred image and you get a larger blur, not more detail. A light microscope cannot resolve below about **200 nm** however much it magnifies, and that is why organelles such as ribosomes were invisible before the electron microscope.

**The electron microscope resolves to about 0.2 nm** — roughly **1000 times** finer. It was that jump, not the magnification, that revealed the internal structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts, and made ribosomes and plasmids visible at all.

**And there is a trade-off.** An electron microscope is **large and expensive**, the specimen must be in a **vacuum** so it cannot be **alive**, and the image is **black and white** with colour added afterwards. A light microscope is cheap, portable, and shows **living** specimens in colour. Neither replaces the other.

steps.title: Units, prefixes and standard form
steps.body:
**Cells are measured in units most people never use**, so the spec asks you to know them and to convert between them.

- **milli (m)** — $10^{-3}$ — a thousandth
- **micro (µ)** — $10^{-6}$ — a millionth
- **nano (n)** — $10^{-9}$ — a thousand-millionth
- **pico (p)** — $10^{-12}$

**Each prefix is three powers of ten below the last**, so each step of the ladder is **×1000**:

$$1\text{ mm} = 1000\ \unicode{181}\text{m} = 1\,000\,000\text{ nm}$$

**Going down the ladder, multiply by 1000. Going up, divide by 1000.** That is the whole conversion skill, and almost every lost mark in this topic comes from doing it the wrong way round or forgetting it entirely.

**Standard form** keeps these numbers manageable. A cell 0.000 06 m across is $6 \times 10^{-5}$ m, which is easier to compare with another number than counting zeros is.

**A sense of scale worth carrying:**

- an animal cell — about **10 to 30 µm** across
- a bacterium — about **1 to 5 µm**
- a ribosome — about **20 nm**

**Estimating.** The spec asks you to **use estimations and explain when they should be used**. An estimate is right when you want to know whether an answer is **plausible** — is this cell nearer 10 µm or 10 mm? — and wrong when the question asks you to **calculate**. Use it to check, not to replace working.

steps.title: The magnification equation
steps.body:
**One equation covers every calculation in this topic:**

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$

**Magnification has no unit**, because it is one length divided by another — but only when **both lengths are in the same unit**. Converting first is not optional.

Rearranged, it answers the other two questions: $\text{actual size} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}$, and $\text{image size} = \text{magnification} \times \text{actual size}$.

steps.title: Core practical: using a microscope
steps.body:
**This is core practical 1**, and the method is examinable.

**Preparing the slide:**

1. Put a drop of **water** on a clean slide.
2. Add the **thin** specimen — a single layer of onion epidermis, or cheek cells on a cotton bud. **Thin matters**: light has to pass through it.
3. Add a **stain**. **Iodine** for plant cells, **methylene blue** for animal cells. The stain makes otherwise colourless structures, especially the **nucleus**, visible.
4. Lower the **coverslip at an angle**, using a mounted needle. This is so **air bubbles** are pushed out rather than trapped — a bubble looks like a cell with a thick dark edge and is a classic misidentification.

**Focusing:**

1. Start on the **lowest power** objective, so the field of view is widest and the specimen is easiest to find.
2. Use the **coarse** focus first, then the **fine** focus.
3. Only then switch to a higher power objective and refocus with the **fine** knob alone.

**Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.** A ×10 eyepiece with a ×40 objective gives **×400**.

**The drawing** is marked as much as the observing:

- **sharp pencil**, **clear unbroken lines**, and **no shading**
- draw **what you see**, not what the textbook shows
- **label lines straight**, drawn with a ruler, **not crossing** each other
- a **title** and the **magnification** stated

steps.title: Reading a question about size
steps.body:
**Most marks in this topic are lost on the unit, not on the arithmetic.** Three habits fix that.

**1. Write the equation before you touch the numbers.** It tells you which way round the division goes. The commonest error is $\dfrac{\text{actual}}{\text{image}}$, which gives a number below 1 — and a magnification below 1 means the image is **smaller** than the object, which a microscope does not do. That is a free check.

**2. Convert first, then calculate.** Bring both lengths to the same unit before dividing. If the question asks for an answer in µm and your image was measured in mm, convert **at the end** as a separate step, so you can see it.

**3. Ask whether the answer is a believable size.** A cell of 60 µm is reasonable. A cell of 60 mm is six centimetres and would be visible from across the room. A ribosome of 20 nm is right; 20 µm would make it the size of a whole cell. The estimate does not replace the calculation — it tells you when to look for a slipped thousand.

**What the estimate is for.** The spec asks you to explain **when** an estimate should be used. It is for **checking plausibility** and for **comparing orders of magnitude** — not for answering a question that says *calculate*.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Resolution is the real story of microscope technology.** Magnification alone is almost free — you can enlarge any image. What limits you is **resolution**: the smallest separation that still shows as two things. A light microscope stops at about **200 nm**, and no lamp or lens gets past it. The electron microscope reaches about **0.2 nm**, about **1000 times** finer, and that is why organelles appeared. An answer crediting the discovery of ribosomes to higher magnification has the wrong cause.

**And say what the new detail bought us.** The spec's wording is that better microscopes **increased our understanding of the role of sub-cellular structures**. Seeing the inside of a mitochondrion is what let anyone work out what it does. Technology changed the biology, not just the pictures.

**A magnification below 1 is impossible, so it is a free check.** If your answer says the image is smaller than the object, you either divided the wrong way round or missed a unit conversion. Checks that catch an error **without your knowing the right answer** are the most valuable kind, and this topic has two: this one and the plausibility of the size.

**Convert as a visible, separate step.** Doing the conversion in your head and writing only the final number means a slipped factor of a thousand is invisible to you and to the examiner — and a method mark that could have been rescued is lost with it.

**Know when an estimate is the right tool.** The spec asks for this explicitly. An estimate settles **order of magnitude**: is this a cell or an organelle? It does not answer a question that says *calculate*, and offering one there earns nothing.

**Draw what is on the slide.** Marks for a biological drawing are for **accuracy of what you observed** and for the conventions — **unbroken pencil lines, no shading, ruled label lines that do not cross, a title and the magnification**. A beautiful textbook diagram of a cell you could not actually resolve is worth less than a plain, honest one.

- Better **resolution**, not magnification, is what revealed organelles.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between magnification and resolution, and evaluate what the development of the electron microscope allowed biologists to do that a light microscope could not.
questions.solution:
**Magnification** is how many times **larger the image is than the object**: an image 1000 times the width of a cell has been magnified ×1000. **Resolution** is a different quantity altogether — the **smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as two separate points** rather than one.

The two are often confused, but only one of them limits what can be seen. **Magnification is cheap**: any image can be enlarged. What cannot be recovered is detail that was never **resolved** — enlarging an unresolved image simply produces a **larger blur**. So resolution, not magnification, is what decides whether a structure is visible at all.

This is why the **electron microscope** mattered. A light microscope resolves to about **200 nm** and no lamp or lens improves on that. An electron microscope resolves to about **0.2 nm**, roughly **1000 times finer**. Structures that had been below the limit became visible: **ribosomes**, at about 20 nm, **plasmids**, and the **internal structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts**. As the specification puts it, this **increased our understanding of the role of sub-cellular structures** — seeing inside a mitochondrion is what allowed anyone to work out what it does.

It did not make the light microscope obsolete, though. An electron microscope is **very large and expensive**, and its specimens must be held in a **vacuum**, so they **cannot be alive** and cannot be watched moving; the images are **black and white**, with any colour added afterwards. A light microscope is cheap, portable, and shows **living** cells. Each answers questions the other cannot, so the right conclusion is that the electron microscope **extended** what could be seen rather than replacing the older instrument.

questions.prompt: A student prepares a slide of onion cells and calculates the magnification of their drawing. Describe the method they should follow, and explain the checks that would tell them their calculation was wrong.
questions.solution:
The student puts a **drop of water** on a clean slide and adds a **thin** piece of onion epidermis — thin because light has to pass through it. They add a drop of **iodine**, which stains the otherwise colourless structures, and in particular makes the **nucleus** visible. They then lower the **coverslip at an angle** with a mounted needle.

To find the magnification of their drawing they use $\text{magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$, having first put **both lengths in the same unit**. This is where the marks are usually lost: an image measured in **millimetres** divided by an actual size in **micrometres** gives an answer a **thousand** times out.

Two checks catch that without knowing the right answer. First, a **magnification below 1** is impossible — it would mean the microscope had made the cell **smaller** — so such an answer means the division was inverted or a conversion was missed. Second, the actual size should be a **plausible** size for the object: a plant cell is roughly **50 to 100 µm**, so an answer of 50 mm is wrong by a factor of a thousand and an answer of 50 nm is wrong the other way. Checks that work without the answer are the most useful ones there are.

questions.modelAnswer:
The student puts a **drop of water** on a clean slide and adds a **thin** piece of onion epidermis — thin because light has to pass through it. They add a drop of **iodine**, which stains the otherwise colourless structures, and in particular makes the **nucleus** visible. They then lower the **coverslip at an angle** with a mounted needle.

That last step has a reason worth giving: lowering it at an angle **pushes air out ahead of the liquid** rather than trapping it. A trapped **air bubble** appears as a round shape with a thick dark edge and is regularly mistaken for a cell, so an avoidable bubble can spoil the observation entirely.

To view the slide they start on the **lowest power objective**, because that gives the **widest field of view** and makes the specimen easy to find. They focus with the **coarse** knob first and then the **fine** knob, and only then move to a higher power, refocusing with the **fine** knob alone.

To find the magnification of their drawing they use $\text{magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$, having first put **both lengths in the same unit**. This is where the marks are usually lost: an image measured in **millimetres** divided by an actual size in **micrometres** gives an answer a **thousand** times out.

Two checks catch that without knowing the right answer. First, a **magnification below 1** is impossible — it would mean the microscope had made the cell **smaller** — so such an answer means the division was inverted or a conversion was missed. Second, the actual size should be a **plausible** size for the object: a plant cell is roughly **50 to 100 µm**, so an answer of 50 mm is wrong by a factor of a thousand and an answer of 50 nm is wrong the other way. Checks that work without the answer are the most useful ones there are.

examTechnique.body:
This topic is examined as **calculation plus care**. The biology is short — magnification, resolution, the units, and one practical — and nearly every lost mark is a **unit** rather than a misunderstanding. Write the equation, convert both lengths to the same unit as a **separate visible step**, then divide.

The other half is the **core practical**. Learn the method as a sequence of steps **with reasons**, because the questions ask why: why a thin specimen, why a stain, why the coverslip goes down at an angle, why you start at low power.
examinerErrors: Dividing **mm by µm** without converting, so the answer is out by a factor of a **thousand**.
Dividing **actual by image** instead of image by actual, giving a magnification **below 1**.
Saying the electron microscope revealed organelles because of higher **magnification**, when it was better **resolution**.
Using **magnification** and **resolution** as if they meant the same thing.
Giving the **total magnification** as eyepiece **plus** objective rather than **multiplied** by it.
Omitting the reason for lowering the coverslip at an angle — **avoiding air bubbles**.
Shading a biological drawing, or drawing the textbook cell rather than the one on the slide.
Offering an **estimate** when the question said **calculate**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats **resolution** as the point of the whole topic: it explains that unresolved detail cannot be recovered by enlarging, quotes roughly **200 nm against 0.2 nm**, and names what became visible — ribosomes at about 20 nm, plasmids, the inside of a mitochondrion. In calculations it converts units as a **separate written step**, so a slipped thousand is visible, and it checks the answer two ways: a magnification **below 1 is impossible**, and the actual size must be a **plausible** size for that object. Asked to evaluate the electron microscope, it gives the cost, the size and the **vacuum** that rules out living specimens, and concludes that the two instruments answer different questions.
